allergens.label: Milk
allergens.notes: Specific phrases come before the bare word they contain, because the first match wins and is the term shown as evidence: "ice cream" must precede "cream", and the qualified milks precede "milk". Cheeses are named individually: matching is by word token, so "cheese" cannot catch "mozzarella". The exclusions carry the plant-based analogues, which is what keeps bare "milk", "cream", "butter", "curd" and "dairy" safe to list as definite terms. "mustard" is excluded for the same reason as under EGGS: it is one edit away from "custard". "natural flavour" is deliberately absent, here and under EGGS, SOY and FISH: Canada's 2012 allergen labelling amendments (Food and Drug Regulations B.01.010.1-.3) require a priority allergen to be declared even when it is a component of a flavouring, which is precisely the gap they closed, so a bare "natural flavour" on a compliant label is not concealing one. It also appears on so much of the grocery shelf that listing it put four POSSIBLE warnings on a plain soda and a fish warning on strawberry jam - the same objection, and the same conclusion, as PEANUTS and "vegetable oil".

allergens.label: Eggs
allergens.notes: "custard" is listed here as well as under MILK: it is both. The egg-prefixed phrases precede bare "egg" so the evidence quoted is the specific one. "mustard" is excluded because it is one edit away from "custard", which the fuzzy near-miss pass would otherwise read as a possible egg on every mustard label. "natural flavour" is absent for the reason set out under MILK.

allergens.label: Peanuts
allergens.notes: "vegetable oil" is deliberately absent: Canadian labelling requires peanut oil to be declared as peanut, so a generic "vegetable oil" is canola, soy or corn and would warn on almost every packaged food. The unqualified nut words stay ambiguous rather than definite, since mixed nuts and nut butters often but not always include peanuts.

allergens.label: Tree nuts
allergens.notes: "hickory nut", not bare "hickory": on a label "hickory" is almost always smoke flavouring from the wood. "coconut" stays ambiguous because Canada does not treat it as a tree nut while the United States does. "butternut" is left out on purpose - butternut squash is far commoner than the nut.

allergens.label: Soy
allergens.notes: "textured vegetable protein" is a definite term, not an ambiguous one: TVP is soy protein by definition. "vegetable oil" does belong here as ambiguous, unlike under PEANUTS, because soybean oil is the commonest generic vegetable oil. "natural flavour" is absent for the reason set out under MILK.

allergens.label: Wheat/Gluten
allergens.notes: Bare "flour" is a definite term, not an ambiguous one, and it is the only bare word here that is: under Division 13 of the Food and Drug Regulations (B.13.001) "flour", "white flour", "enriched flour" and "plain flour" are standardised names for the product of milling wheat, so unqualified "flour" on a Canadian label is wheat by law rather than by likelihood. That makes the exclusion list load-bearing in a way it was not before: every common non-wheat flour must be listed there or it now produces a firm CONTAINS rather than a soft warning, so add to it when a new one shows up. Promoting the term caught "mustard flour" claiming wheat on the spot, which is how the list came to cover the nut, legume, seed and rye-and-barley flours as well; it still cannot be exhaustive, and the accepted cost is that a flour nobody has listed yet over-warns. That is the tolerable direction - a wheat-avoidant user skips a safe food - and the direction that matters, missing wheat that is present, is unaffected, since "wheat" and "wheat flour" are definite terms in their own right. The same list also guards bare "bran" and "noodle", which stay ambiguous because they have no such standard of identity. "starch", "modified starch", "modified food starch", "malt extract" and "dextrin" were removed for the reason given under MUSTARD: wheat is both a priority allergen and a gluten source, so a wheat-derived starch or dextrin must be declared as wheat, and those terms fired on most packaged savoury food without finding anything. "sans gluten" is kept as a false-positive guard: "gluten" is an English term, and French negates before the noun so the trailing-"free" rule cannot catch it. This entry covers gluten as well as wheat, which is what the label "Wheat/Gluten" says and is why barley, rye, oats, triticale and the malts are all definite terms here: B.01.010.1 names exactly those grains as Canada's gluten sources, and oats are on that list despite being gluten-free botanically. An earlier version left them out and said so in this note, on the reasoning that they would need an allergen of their own - which would be defensible if the label promised only wheat, and is not, because it promises gluten. Their flours must therefore never be excluded: "oat flour", "oat bran", "rye flour" and "barley flour" were all in the exclusion list and all suppressed a real gluten source, which is the one direction this file must never fail in. "gluten free oat" is excluded instead, since certified gluten-free oats are a real product and the trailing-"free" rule only catches "oats free". The id stays WHEAT: it is the key the saved allergen selections are stored under, so renaming it would silently drop every existing user's choice. "brewer s yeast" is spelled that way on purpose, the same trick "za atar" uses under SESAME: normalisation turns every run of non-alphanumerics into a space, so "brewer's yeast" arrives as three tokens and the two-word phrase cannot reach it. "beer", "ale", "lager" and "stout" are definite because beer batter and stout cakes are real, with "root beer" and "ginger beer" excluded as the two soft drinks that merely borrow the word. Distilled spirits are deliberately absent: distillation removes gluten, so whisky is not a source even when it is made from malt.

allergens.label: Sesame
allergens.notes: "spice", "spice blend" and "seasoning" were removed for the reason given under MUSTARD: sesame is a priority allergen and must be declared by name even inside a class-name ingredient, so those three could only ever fire on savoury products without finding anything. What is left is the "is it, maybe" case - dishes that are substantially sesame rather than dishes sesame might hide in. "bagel" and "bun" are a judgement about toppings, not about hidden components: the seeds are on the outside and often absent from the ingredient list altogether.

allergens.label: Fish
allergens.notes: Species whose name ends in "fish" are each listed: matching is by word token, so the term "fish" does not catch "monkfish". "swedish fish" is excluded because the candy contains none. "natural flavour" is absent for the reason set out under MILK; the fish-derived flavourings worth naming are named, as "worcestershire" and "caesar".

allergens.label: Shellfish
allergens.notes: Covers both of Canada's shellfish groups, crustaceans and molluscs. "oyster mushroom" is a fungus and "crab apple" a fruit, hence the exclusions.

allergens.label: Mustard
allergens.notes: The ambiguous list is empty on purpose, and should stay empty. It held thirteen terms - "curry powder", "curry", "spice", "seasoning", "vinaigrette", "relish", "pickle", "chutney", "remoulade", "barbecue sauce", "bbq sauce", "salad dressing", "marinade" - and every one of them was the same mistake as "natural flavour" under MILK: each names a compound ingredient that might contain mustard as an undeclared component, and under Canada's 2012 amendments there is no such thing. Mustard became a priority allergen through those very amendments, so it must be declared by name wherever it occurs, including inside a class-name ingredient such as "spices" or "seasoning". The list therefore could not catch anything a compliant label hides, while firing on most condiments and savoury snacks on the shelf: it put a mustard warning on plain salad dressing, barbecue chips and instant noodles. A term earns a place here only if it is a generic name for mustard itself - the "is it, maybe" case that "mixed nuts" is for PEANUTS - not if it is a food that mustard might be hiding inside.
